blocks.html: Johannes Gutenberg (c. 1400–1468) was a goldsmith and metalworker from Mainz, a city on the Rhine in Germany. We know his life mostly from legal and money records: loans, lawsuits and contracts. No letter or book by him in his own words survives. What survives is his work: the Bible he printed in Mainz around 1454–1455, of which about 49 copies still exist, some of them complete.

Gutenberg's invention was a system: a hand mould that cast many identical metal letters quickly, a metal mix that melted easily and set hard, an oil-based ink that stuck to metal, and a screw press to push paper evenly onto the inked type. Together they made printing fast, cheap and exact.

Before printing, every book in Europe was copied by hand. A scribe might take months to copy one Bible. Printing from carved wooden blocks was already known in Europe for pictures and short texts, and in China and Korea people had printed books for centuries, including with movable type in clay (Bi Sheng, 1040s) and metal (Korea, 1200s and 1300s). But carving a whole block for every page is slow, and European writing, with its small alphabet, suited a different approach: make each letter once, as a reusable piece, and arrange them into any page.

Gutenberg knew metal casting from goldsmith work. The hard part was making thousands of letters that were all exactly the same height, so every one would touch the paper. His answer was the hand mould: a two-part metal box with a slot. Into the bottom he set a matrix, a small copper block with a letter punched into it. Pour in hot metal, open the mould, and out comes a sort, one piece of type. Change the matrix and the same mould makes the next letter.

items: Type metal: mostly lead, with tin and antimony. Lead melts at a low heat; tin helps it flow; antimony makes it hard and keeps it from shrinking as it cools, so the letters stay sharp.
Ink: the water-based inks scribes used would run off metal. Gutenberg used an oil-based ink, more like a varnish with soot, similar to the oil paints painters used.
The press: a big wooden screw press, like the presses used to squeeze grapes for wine or olives for oil, pressed the paper or vellum evenly onto the type.

blocks.name: iv-mirror
blocks.cap: Type a word. A piece of type is a mirror image of the letter, so it prints the right way round. Press Print to see the page.

blocks.html: Type is a stamp. When you press a stamp onto paper, left and right swap. So the letters on the type are carved backward, and the printed page comes out forward. Typesetters learned to read backward, and set lines from left to right holding the type upside down in a composing stick.

blocks.text: What he tried, and what failed

blocks.html: Gutenberg worked on his ideas in Strasbourg in the late 1430s, where a lawsuit of 1439 mentions a secret project with a press, metal "forms" and lead. Back in Mainz he borrowed large sums from a merchant named Johann Fust. Printing a big Bible took years and cost a fortune in paper, vellum and metal before a single copy could be sold. In 1455 Fust sued for his money, and much of the workshop seems to have passed to Fust and Gutenberg's skilled helper Peter Schöffer. They went on to print books under their own names. Gutenberg's great invention did not make him rich.

blocks.html: The Gutenberg Bible has 42 lines on most pages, set in two columns, in a type designed to look like the best handwriting. About 180 copies were printed, most on paper and some on vellum (calfskin). Each copy was then decorated by hand, so no two look exactly alike.

blocks.title: Copies and pages
blocks.q: A Bible has 1,282 pages. A print shop prints 180 copies. How many printed pages is that in all?

blocks.html:
📖 Story or history?

Nobody knows exactly when Gutenberg first printed with movable type, or exactly what his first printed item was. Small items like a poem and indulgences (printed forms) came before the Bible. Dates like "1440" or "1450" in many books are estimates. Historians are confident about the Mainz Bible of about 1454–1455.

Printing presses in over 200 European towns

blocks.html: Printing spread across Europe within fifty years. Books became cheaper, more people learned to read, and scholars could all work from the same exact text instead of copies full of different errors. Scientists could share drawings and tables that stayed correct from copy to copy. Many historians tie printing to the Renaissance, the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution, though they debate how much it caused and how much it helped along.

Saying Gutenberg invented printing. Printing, and even movable type, came first in East Asia. Gutenberg's achievement was a practical system of casting, ink and press that made printing fast in Europe.

Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519) was born near the town of Vinci, outside Florence. He trained as a painter in the workshop of Andrea del Verrocchio, then worked in Milan, Florence, Rome and finally France. We know him for paintings like the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper. He also filled thousands of notebook pages with studies of water, birds, the human body, light and machines.

Leonardo learned by looking hard and drawing what he saw, then asking how it worked. His notebooks hold designs for flying machines, pumps, bridges and gears. Most were never built in his lifetime, and some would not have worked as drawn. Their value is in the questions and the careful observation.

About 7,000 pages of his notes survive, scattered across collections; many more were lost. He wrote most of them in mirror writing, from right to left, so they are easiest to read in a mirror. He was left-handed, and writing right to left kept him from smearing the ink. He rarely finished a treatise, and the notes were not published in his lifetime.

blocks.html: Leonardo trusted what he could test over what old books said. In the notebooks he wrote:

Leonardo watched birds and bats for years and wrote a small notebook on the flight of birds around 1505. He drew machines where a person would flap wings with arms and legs, and a screw-shaped device often called his helicopter. His notes show him thinking about balance and how the wing should be built.

People are not strong enough to fly by flapping. Our arm and leg muscles are far weaker for our weight than a bird's chest muscles. Leonardo seems to have come to doubt flapping too, and later drawings lean toward gliding. There is no good evidence that any of his flying machines left the ground. The idea that worked came four centuries later: fixed wings for lift, a separate engine for push, and controls for balance.

blocks.text: The eye and the dark room

blocks.html: Leonardo compared the eye to a dark room with a small hole, following the optics of Ibn al-Haytham that had reached Europe in Latin.

blocks.cap: The same dark room Leonardo describes: the image on the far wall is upside down.

blocks.html:
📖 Story or history?

You may see models labeled "Leonardo's tank" or "Leonardo's helicopter." These were built in modern times from his drawings, often with changes to make them work. In his own day they stayed on paper. His studies of anatomy and water were far ahead of his time; his machines are best seen as ideas.

blocks.title: How old?
blocks.q: Leonardo was born in 1452 and wrote his notebook on bird flight around 1505. About how old was he?

blocks.html: Because his notes were scattered and unpublished, Leonardo's machines had little direct effect on later engineers. His deeper legacy is a way of working: observe closely, draw exactly, ask how it works, and test ideas against nature. The Wright brothers, four hundred years later, also started by watching birds.

Thinking Leonardo's designs were working inventions. Most are untested sketches. Some, like his studies of gears and pulleys, were sound; others, like a person-powered flapping machine, could not fly.
